title: Start
text: Tap or press any key to begin. Headphones recommended.

title: Welcome
text: Welcome to Feel the Earth, your Earth information jukebox. Get ready to experience the world through sound! I'm Jodi, your personal guide, and I'm going to walk you through this journey with my voice. Every single note you hear from now on is data collected by NASA. You can explore all kinds of maps by ear, like ocean currents and sea surface temperature, night lights, lightning seen from the space station, aerosols, and many more. Here's how the map speaks to you. Imagine a listening window resting over the globe. Every few seconds, a scan sweeps across that window from west to east, from your left ear to your right ear. As the scan moves, real Earth data is turned into music.

title: Welcome
text: Whenever you're ready, press T, or hold J and say tutorial, for a guided listening tour. Press shift and T, or say assistant tour, to learn how to talk to me. And if you already know the map, just tap J to turn my voice off.

title: Listening tour
text: Welcome to the listening tour! Everything you hear is NASA Earth data turned into music. I'll play each sound, light it up on the map, and tell you why it sounds the way it does. Press Escape any time to stop.

title: The scan
text: This is the music of the place under your listening window. A bright line sweeps across the window from west to east, once every four bars. Wherever it passes, that slice of data becomes a note, and the cells it reads light up. West is in your left ear, east is in your right.

title: Height is pitch
text: Height on the map becomes height in pitch. Features in the north of the window sound higher, features in the south sound lower. Listen to a feature moving from south to north.

title: Value is loudness
text: Bigger values play louder and brighter. Here's a low value, a middle value, and a high value.

title: 1 · Sea surface temperature
text: Key one is sea surface temperature, played by the cello section. Cold water sounds thin and icy. Warm water sounds dark and full, because a warmer ocean holds more energy. First cold water, then warm.

title: 2 · Lightning
text: Key two is lightning, played by the glockenspiel and the sound of rain. Each bright strike marks a lightning hot spot, and the rain grows louder where storms are more frequent. First a quiet sky, then a stormy one.

title: 3 · Night lights
text: Key three is night lights, played by the harp. More and faster harp notes mean more light from towns and cities. It's the sound of people. First countryside, then a city.

title: 4 · Night-light change
text: Key four is night-light change, played by the clarinet. Bright and loud means new lights since 2012. Dark and quiet means lights went out. First lights going out, then new lights.

title: One orchestra
text: Every instrument plays notes from the same chord at the same time. So even data that has nothing to do with each other still sounds like one orchestra, and you can pick out each player.

title: When the Earth is in trouble
text: When the data turns dangerous, like a marine heatwave or a band of violent storms, the music grows darker. A trembling string drone comes in, and at the most severe, a timpani heartbeat. The edges of the screen glow red with it.

title: Crossing the map
text: Moving the window plays quiet signals, so you always know where you are without looking.

title: Border
text: Two wooden ticks mean you crossed a border into another country.

title: Coast
text: A wave means you left land for the sea. A soft drum means you reached land.

title: Equator
text: A singing bowl means you crossed the equator into the other hemisphere.

title: Tropics and meridians
text: A small bell marks the tropics and the polar circles. A lower bell marks the prime meridian.

title: Date line
text: A rising, reversed cymbal means you crossed the date line, on the far side of the world.

title: Peaks and valleys
text: While you move, two beacons ping from where the extremes are. Two rising high notes come from the highest value nearby, two falling low notes from the lowest. They get faster as you get closer, and a bell tells you you've arrived. Press B for the peak, or V for the valley.

title: Time
text: A clock tick steps one day forward. A wind chime steps one month.

title: Your turn
text: That's the tour! Use the arrow keys to explore. Press H to hear what's playing right now, W for where you are, and T to take this tour again. To learn how to talk to me, press shift and T.

title: Talking to Jodi
text: Here's how to talk to me. Press and hold J, or simply say hey Jodi, then tell me what you'd like. Let go of J when you've finished speaking.

title: Moving around
text: To move around the Earth, hold J and say a direction, like north, or far east. Or jump straight to a place: say take me to India, or fly to the Pacific. You can change the size of your listening area too. Just say wider, narrower, or whole world.

title: Where am I?
text: Ask me where am I, or what am I hearing, and I'll tell you where you are on the map and what you're listening to. The keys W and H do the same.

title: Layers
text: You can focus on different layers any time. Hold J and say what you'd like to hear, like ocean, air temperature, lightning, carbon dioxide, or vegetation. Say next layer to cycle through them one by one.

title: Hunting extremes
text: Fancy hunting for extremes? Press B, or say find the peak. You'll hear two rising notes pinging from the direction of the highest value nearby. Just follow the sound until a bright bell tells you you've arrived. Press V, or say find the valley, for the lowest.

title: Time travel
text: You aren't stuck in one day. Hold J and say next month, or previous year, or say time travel to hear the climate and the city lights change over time.

title: Ask me anything
text: And you can just ask me things, like why is the sea so warm here? I'll answer from the data you're hearing.

title: Enjoy!
text: If you miss any of this, no worries! Say help any time to hear this guide again. Now go on, enjoy!
